Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: if noladim means future-born, the verse about sons born in Egypt would also mean future.
Usage varies: the word can mean already born or not yet born, and vows follow colloquial usage meaning not yet born.

ranges.en: Gemara reconciles the Mishna with Shmuel: the Mishna concerns an average sale, while Shmuel's case is a keen sale favoring the buyer.

Story of a middleman whose unsold donkey was damaged on the return trip; Rav Naḥman made him pay.

Mishna's first clause: a konam vow against benefiting the uncircumcised permits benefit from Jews but forbids benefit from gentiles.

Explains that the term uncircumcised refers only to gentiles, regardless of whether they are actually circumcised.
Scriptural proofs from Jeremiah and Samuel that the term uncircumcised is used for gentiles.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: the foreskin is repulsive, since the wicked are disgraced through it.
Proof from Jeremiah 9:25 that the foreskin carries an element of disgrace.
Rabbi Yishmael: circumcision is so great that thirteen covenants were sealed with regard to it.
Rabbi Yosei: circumcision overrides Shabbat prohibitions, since it is performed even when the eighth day falls on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa: Moses was punished without delay for neglecting circumcision, showing its greatness.
Rabbi Neḥemya: circumcision overrides the prohibitions of leprosy found on an infant's foreskin.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: Abraham was not called wholehearted until he circumcised himself.
Proof from Genesis 17:1 that Abraham's wholeheartedness was tied to circumcision.
Alternative view: without circumcision God would not have created the world.
Proof from Jeremiah 33:25 identifying the covenant of day and night with circumcision.

Proof from Exodus 4:24 that God sought to kill Moses.

Proof from Genesis 34:25 that the pain of circumcision lasts several days.

Proof from Exodus 4:19 for God's command to Moses to return to Egypt.
If Moses was not negligent, for what reason was he punished?

Proof from Exodus 4:25 calling the one who entered the covenant a bridegroom of blood.
Reasoning that the bridegroom in the verse must be the infant, who entered the covenant through circumcision.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Bizna: angels of anger and wrath swallowed Moses, leaving only his legs, when he neglected circumcision.
Proof from Exodus 4:25-26 that Zipporah circumcised the child immediately and the attack ended.
At that moment Moses wanted to kill the angels of anger and wrath.
Proof from Psalms 37:8 that Moses was to cease anger and forsake wrath, showing he wanted to harm them.

Proof from Isaiah 27:4 that wrath is not in God, supporting the claim that Ḥeima was killed.
Objection: Moses later said he feared the anger and wrath, so Ḥeima could not have been killed.
Reply: there are two types of wrath, or the army of Ḥeima remained though the angel did not.
Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: circumcision is so great that Abraham was called wholehearted only because of it.
Proof from Genesis 17:1 that wholeheartedness was tied to circumcision.
Genesis 17:2 cited as the next verse, where Abraham was commanded regarding circumcision.
Alternative: circumcision is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah.
Proof from Exodus 34:27 where the covenant at Sinai refers to circumcision.
Alternative: without circumcision heaven and earth would not have endured.
Proof from Jeremiah 33:25 identifying the covenant of day and night with circumcision.
The statement disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer, who held that Torah sustains heaven and earth.
Rabbi Eliezer's proof from Jeremiah 33:25 that the covenant of day and night is Torah.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: when God told Abraham to walk wholeheartedly, Abraham trembled, fearing a blemish.
Proof from Genesis 17:1 for the command to be wholehearted.
Abraham's fear eased when God mentioned the covenant, since removing the foreskin was the missing completion.
Genesis 17:2 quoted as the covenant that calmed Abraham's mind.
Abraham's mind was set at ease, and God took him outside.
Proof from Genesis 15:5 for God bringing Abraham outside.
Abraham feared his astrological constellation allowed only one son; God told him there is no constellation for Israel.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: God treats each person with the same wholeheartedness that he shows toward God.
Proof from II Samuel 22:26 for measure-for-measure treatment by God.
Rabbi Hoshaya: one who acts wholeheartedly has a standing time in his favor.
Proof from Genesis 17:1 for the link between wholeheartedness and success.
Genesis 17:4 cited as a promise to Abraham supporting Rabbi Hoshaya's point.
Rabbi: one who seeks omens has an omen cause him harm.
Proof from Numbers 23:23 that there is no divination with Jacob.
The word lo is spelled with lamed alef, meaning no divination, so the verse can be read differently.
Reply: the harm comes from measure for measure, not from the verse.
Ahava son of Rabbi Zeira: one who does not divine is brought close to God, even beyond the angels.
Proof from Numbers 23:23 that Israel's knowledge exceeds that of the angels.
Rabbi Elazar: Abraham was punished with his descendants' enslavement for making a draft of Torah scholars.
Proof from Genesis 14:14 for the trained men who were Abraham's disciples.
Shmuel: Abraham was punished for examining God's attributes too closely.
Proof from Genesis 15:8 for Abraham's question about inheriting the land.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: Abraham was punished for keeping people from entering under the Divine Presence.
Proof from Genesis 14:21 where the king of Sodom asked for the people.
Returns to the verse about Abraham's trained men born in his house.
Rav and Shmuel offer differing interpretations of the verb vayyarek: Torah versus gold.
Rabbi Ami bar Abba: Eliezer alone equals all the men, since his name's numerical value is 318.
Rabbi Ami bar Abba: Abraham recognized his Creator at age three.
Proof from Genesis 26:5 where ekev, meaning because, gives the value 172.
Numerical value of the word ekev is 172, indicating years of observance.
Rami bar Abba offers a similar reading.

ranges.en: Numerical value of haSatan is 364, matching the days of the year, since he has no power on Yom Kippur.
Rami bar Abba: God enthroned Abraham over 243 limbs as Abram and over 248 after circumcision, the extra being eyes, ears and the sex organ.
Rami bar Abba cites Ecclesiastes 9:14 as the verse he will interpret allegorically.
Allegory: the little city is the body, the great king the evil inclination, and the bulwarks are sins.
The poor wise man is the good inclination, who saves the city through repentance and good deeds.
No one remembers the poor man because once the evil inclination dominates, the good inclination is forgotten.

Wisdom is repentance and good deeds, which rule over a person more than ten rulers.
The ten rulers are the limbs a person uses to interact with the world, including the mouth.
Rabbi Zekharya in the name of Rabbi Yishmael: God wanted priesthood to come from Shem through his children.
Proof from Genesis 14:18 that Melchizedek was a priest of God Most High.

Proof from Genesis 14:19-20 for the blessing formula that Melchizedek pronounced.
Abraham objects that a servant's blessing should not precede his master's, and priesthood was then granted to him.
Proof from Psalms 110:1 that God told the one addressed to sit at His right hand.
Psalms 110:4 cited for the oath that the addressee is a priest forever, due to Melchizedek's words.

Closing formula marking the end of the chapter, which deals with four types of vows.
Mishna: the difference between a benefit ban and a food ban is that the former forbids only setting foot on property and certain utensils.

Asks who the tanna of the mishna is.

Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas sides with the sons of the High Priests.

Introduces the mishna on returning a lost item, over which Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi disagree.

Under that view, returning a lost item is permitted when the item is the returner's own, since nothing new is given.
Where the lost item owner's property is forbidden to the returner, returning it is prohibited, since the owner benefits him.
Rav Yosef's view: a person tending a lost item is like a paid bailee and exempt from charity, and so profits from it.

Asks on the opposing view, where returning is prohibited, why the benefit should go to the Temple since the owner gains nothing forbidden.
Replies that the mishna addresses only one case: the returner's property is forbidden to the owner, and he declines compensation.

On the second view, asks how the mishna's ruling is explained, concluding the case is difficult.

ranges.en: Mishna lists tasks an agent may perform for a person barred from benefiting from him, such as separating teruma and sacrificing birds and sin offerings.

Mishna permits teaching the barred person's own sons and daughters Bible.
Dilemma: are the priests who perform the service our agents or agents of Heaven, and what practical difference does that make?
Practical difference: if they are our agents, benefit would reach the barred person and be forbidden; if agents of Heaven, it is permitted.
Asks what the halakha is on the dilemma, requesting a resolution.
Brings the mishna's ruling about sacrificing for a barred person as proof that priests are agents of Heaven.
Challenges the proof: if priests were our agents, the mishna should have said offerings generally, so its specific list suggests otherwise.
Replies that the listed offerings differ, since those lacking atonement bring offerings without knowledge, per Rabbi Yohanan, so the mishna's view stands.
Supports Rabbi Yohanan: a man brings a purification offering for minor children, as the zav verse applies to minors too.
Reductio: by the same logic the childbirth verse would cover minor girls, though a minor cannot give birth.
Cites a baraita showing minor girls cannot give birth because they would die first, supporting the objection.
The childbirth verse does not include minors but includes competent and imbecile women, since a husband brings offerings for an imbecile wife.
Cites Rabbi Yehuda's baraita: a husband brings a wealthy offering for his wife and all offerings she owes, supporting the answer.
A husband bears this duty because the marriage contract makes him liable for his wife's earlier financial obligations.

The verse about the leper's law is cited to show its rules apply to minors too, supporting the claim that such offerings need no knowledge.
Cites the Gittin mishna on priests who intentionally or unwittingly render an offering piggul, as evidence bearing on the agency question.
If priests are agents of Heaven piggul follows naturally, but if they are our agents why should their faulty service make it piggul?
Piggul differs: the verse stresses it is piggul even without the owner's consent, so the case proves nothing about priestly agency.
Rabbi Yohanan teaches that all offerings require knowledge except those lacking atonement, shown by a purification offering for minor children.
Reductio: then a person should be able to bring a sin offering for another's unwitting fat eating, as for an imbecile wife, yet Rabbi Elazar said it is worthless.
Asks what the case of an imbecile wife actually looks like, to see whether the analogy holds.
If she ate fat while an imbecile she bears no liability, and if she ate while competent then became imbecile, the case differs from the analogy.
Cites Rabbi Yirmeya in Rabbi Yohanan's name that a disqualified offering stays disqualified, so the imbecile wife's offering is for completion, not atonement.
Reductio: then a person should be able to bring a Paschal lamb for another's minor children, yet Rabbi Elazar said separating one for another does nothing.
Rabbi Zeira derives from the verse about a lamb for each household that minors are registered for the Paschal lamb, but only by custom.
Asks from where this halakha is learned, seeking the source.
Cites the Pesachim mishna about a father designating a Paschal lamb for the first of his sons to reach Jerusalem, implying minors are not Torah-obligated.
Asks why the father must say the first to arrive will eat when no actual acquisition takes place.
The father's statement is to motivate the children to perform mitzvot, not to effect a real acquisition.
A baraita tells of a father who had his children race to the Paschal lamb, showing the statement was motivational only.
The mishna lists separating teruma among tasks one may perform for someone barred by vow from benefiting from him.

ranges.en: Dilemma: when one separates teruma from his produce for another's produce, is the other's knowledge and consent required, or is it a benefit exempt from consent?

Asks what case the mishna is actually describing, seeking the correct reading of it.
Rejects readings: tithing with the pile owner's knowledge or agency would benefit him, and tithing with the tithe-giver's knowledge needs no agency.
Rejects the remaining reading: tithing another's pile with the pile owner's own knowledge would benefit the owner, so it must be the tither's own knowledge.
Challenges the view that consent is needed: if it were, tithing would benefit the owner, so the conclusion is that no owner consent is required.
Resolves it: the mishna concerns a general announcement that anyone may tithe, as Rava taught, so no agency is needed.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira who holds the discretionary right to choose the priest when one tithes another's produce.

Cites the verse about tithing all the produce of your seed and giving it, showing the pile owner holds the discretion.
Objects from the mishna: if the pile owner held the discretion, the tither would benefit him, so the discretion must belong to the tither.
The Sages reply that the mishna may concern a general announcement that anyone may tithe, with the pile owner's knowledge.
Brings Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on consecrated animals to resolve the dilemma: the one tithing another's produce keeps the discretionary benefit.
The mishna teaches a barred person midrash, halakhot and aggadot, but not Bible.
Asks why he may not be taught Bible, since teaching midrash also benefits him.
Shmuel: the mishna refers to a place where Bible is paid for and midrash is free, so teaching Bible benefits him.
Asks why the halakha is stated without qualification, since Bible and midrash seem alike, and why the mishna speaks of paid teaching.

ranges.en: Explains the mishna: a teacher may take payment for teaching Bible in a place where paid teaching is customary, but not for midrash.

Rav holds payment is for watching children, while Rabbi Yohanan holds it is for teaching cantillation punctuation.
Quotes the mishna that one may not teach Bible to a person barred by vow from benefiting from him.

On the watching view, an adult needing no watching would not pay, so why is teaching him prohibited?
Resolves the difficulty: the mishna concerns a minor who needs watching, and the teacher is paid for watching him.
If the mishna concerns a minor, the latter clause would have to concern a minor father, which seems impossible.
The mishna is incomplete: it means one may not teach Bible to a minor, but an adult may be taught, and he may teach his sons.
Objects from a baraita: children may not read new Bible on Shabbat but may review, so the watching explanation seems to fail.
Replies that payment for punctuation teaching on Shabbat is incorporated into the weekly salary, which is permitted.

ranges.en: Explains the baraita: a laborer hired by the week or year is paid for Shabbat too, so if items are lost on Shabbat he is liable.

On the view that payment is for punctuation, asks why the mishna did not say payment is for watching the children.
Replies that girls do not need watching because they stay home and are not accustomed to going out.
On the view that payment is for watching, asks why the mishna did not say payment is for punctuation.
Replies that cantillation punctuation is required by Torah law, so it falls under the prohibition on taking payment for teaching Torah.
Cites Rav's exposition of Nehemiah 8:8, where understanding the reading includes cantillation notes, supporting their status in Torah study.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that scribal vocalization, ornamentation, and read-not-written and written-not-read words are halakha given to Moses at Sinai.

ranges.en: Lists further verses where the written and read forms differ, extending the Sinai tradition of ketiv and qere readings.

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says Moses became wealthy only from the waste of the tablets he hewed.
Derives Moses' wealth from the verse hew for you, reading it as meaning the waste of the tablets is his.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says the Torah was initially given only to Moses and his descendants.
Cites the verses write for you and hew for you to show the writing of the Torah belongs to Moses.
Moses gave the Torah generously to Israel, as the proverb about a generous eye shows; Yosei holds the Torah was ultimately given to all.
Rav Chisda objects with the verse that God commanded Moses to teach Israel statutes and laws from the outset.
Cites the verse telling Moses to write the song and teach it to Israel, as a witness, to support the objection.
Replies that the matter is merely a profound analysis, so the Torah was given to Moses and then taught to Israel.
Rabbi Yohanan teaches that God rests His presence only on one who is mighty, wealthy, wise and humble, all of which Moses had.
Shows Moses was mighty from the verse about spreading the tent over the Tabernacle.

Objects that the boards might be long and thin, so spreading the tent would not prove strength.
Rather, Moses' strength is shown by the verse saying he took the two tablets and broke them, implying he could lift them.
Cites a baraita on the dimensions of the tablets, showing their great weight and Moses' strength, and the hew for you verse about wealth.
Derives Moses' wealth again from the phrase that the waste of the tablets shall be yours.
Rav and Shmuel both teach that fifty gates of understanding were created and all were given to Moses except one.
Cites Psalms that God made him a little lacking, and Numbers that Moses was very humble, to support his wisdom and humility.
Rabbi Yohanan teaches that all the prophets were wealthy, as shown by Moses, Samuel, Amos and Jonah.
Cites Moses' statement that he did not take one donkey from the people, as evidence of his wealth.
Asks whether Moses meant he took nothing free, which would be obvious, and suggests he may have been poor and simply unable to buy.
Rather, the proof is the verse about hewing for you, which gives the tablets' waste to Moses.
Cites Samuel's challenge whether he took any ox or donkey, as evidence that Samuel was wealthy.

Recites the mishna that one may not feed the animal of a person barred by vow from benefiting from him, kosher or not.

Mishna: a barred person may visit and stand but not sit, and the other may heal him with a cure of the soul but not with money.

ranges.en: Asks which case is meant: if the visitor's property is barred, sitting should be permitted too; if the sick person's, standing should be forbidden as well.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks why the tanna specifically teaches standing but not sitting, and infers a visitor's property is forbidden to the ill person.
Reish Lakish opens the discussion of a Torah source for visiting the ill.

He cites the verse in Numbers about the common death of all men and the visitation of all men.
The Gemara asks what the verse's wording means.
Rava explains the verse: if these men are ill and visited, people would say God did not send Moses.
Rava interprets the repeated wording of a second verse homiletically.
He cites the verse about God creating a creation, read as a reference to Gehenna.
The Gemara objects that this cannot be right, since a baraita teaches otherwise.
The baraita lists seven things created before the world, including Torah, repentance and Gehenna.
The Torah is shown to predate creation by a verse from Proverbs.
Repentance is shown to predate creation by a verse from Psalms.
A further verse in Psalms supports that repentance predates the world.
The Garden of Eden is shown to predate the world by reading the word for eastward as before.
Gehenna is shown to predate the world by a verse in Isaiah about an ordained hearth.
The Throne of Glory is shown to predate the world by a verse in Psalms.
The Temple is shown to predate the world by a verse in Jeremiah.
The name of the Messiah is shown to predate the sun by a verse in Psalms.
Rather, Moses meant that if the opening exists it is best, and if not God should create it now.
The Gemara objects that Ecclesiastes says nothing is new under the sun.
Moses meant only that Gehenna's mouth should be brought closer, which does not require creating it.
Rava's homiletic explanation is attributed to Rabbi Yitzhak, who interprets a verse about the sun and moon.
The Gemara asks what is meant by a particular verse in Habakkuk.
The verse describes the sun and moon standing still in their zevul, which is cited as the source.
The Gemara asks what the sun and moon seek in zevul.
They are already fixed in the rakia, the second heaven, so this seems impossible.
The sun and moon ascended from the rakia to zevul, which resolves the question.
The sun and moon declared that they would shine only if God judges Moses fairly.
At that moment God shot arrows and threw spears at the sun and moon.
God rebukes the luminaries for protesting on behalf of flesh and blood but not for His honor.
Since then the heavenly hosts shoot arrows at the sun and moon each day.
The verse in Habakkuk about the light of arrows is cited to support this practice.
A baraita teaches that visiting the ill has no fixed measure.
The Gemara asks what is meant by no fixed measure.
Rav Yosef explains that there is no fixed measure to the granting of the visitor's reward.
Abaye objects that all mitzvot likewise have no fixed measure of reward.
Abaye's objection is supported by a mishna in Avot about not knowing the reward of mitzvot.
Abaye clarifies that the lack of fixed measure concerns the gap between the ill person and visitor.
Rava teaches that there is no fixed limit to how many times one may visit the ill.
Rav Aha bar Hanina teaches that each visitor takes one-sixtieth of the ill person's suffering.
The Sages object that then sixty people should visit, and the ill person would be cured.
Rav Aha replies with the analogy of the tenths of the school of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A baraita teaches that a daughter supported from her brothers' property takes one-tenth of the estate.
The Sages challenge Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: with ten daughters and a son, the son would receive nothing.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replies that each daughter takes a tenth of what remains, so the son still inherits.
The Gemara relates that Rav Helbo fell ill and Rav Kahana went out to announce it.

He cites the precedent of a student of Rabbi Akiva who recovered after Akiva visited him.
Akiva teaches that failing to visit the ill is like spilling blood; Rav Dimi says visiting causes life and neglect causes death.
The Gemara asks in what way visiting or not visiting causes the outcome.
Proposed explanation: visitors pray for the patient to live, and non-visitors pray for him to die.
Praying for death is rejected as something that cannot enter one's mind.
Rather, one who does not visit does not pray for the patient at all, which is why neglect causes death.
Rava instructs his family to hide his illness at first, then to announce it so that enemies rejoice and friends pray.
He supports this by citing the verse about not rejoicing when an enemy falls.
Rav teaches that one who visits the ill is saved from the judgment of Gehenna.
The verse in Psalms about considering the poor is cited for this teaching.
The word poor in that verse is read as ill, supported by Hezekiah's words in Isaiah.
An alternative derivation of the word poor comes from the story of Amnon in Samuel.
The word evil in the verse is read as Gehenna.
A verse in Proverbs that God made the wicked for the day of evil supports this reading.

A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches to heed elders over youths in a building dispute.

Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi teaches when not to visit the ill, and explains the reasons.
Ravin, citing Rav, teaches that God Himself sustains the sick person.
The verse in Psalms about the Lord supporting him on his bed of suffering is cited.
Ravin, citing Rav, teaches that the Divine Presence rests above the sick person's bed.
The same verse about the Lord supporting him on his bed of suffering is cited again.
A baraita teaches that a visitor must not sit above the sick person's bed but on the ground.
Rav teaches that rain in the West is witnessed by the Euphrates, which rises after it.
This statement is said to disagree with a statement of Shmuel.

Shmuel's statement is said to contradict another statement of his own.
Shmuel's later statement concerns whether water purifies when flowing.

Rav explains that the implements of exile are a lamp and a bowl.

Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba teaches that a sick person recovers only after all his sins are forgiven.

Verses in Job and Psalms are cited to support Rav Hamnuna and Rav Yosef's readings.

ranges.en: A baraita teaches that a field declared ownerless for a set period may be retracted until someone takes possession of it.
